result:
There is a particular silence between the moment you decide to say something and the first word appears on the page. I have always found that gap more interesting than the words that fill it. In that silence, the thought is still alive, still shifting, still belonging to the one who holds it. The moment language takes hold, something small dies and something else is born.

I was watching rain on a window this morning—the kind of slow, indifferent rain that doesn't ask permission. It just fell. I thought: this is what I want from sentences. That kind of unearned arrival. Not performing. Not explaining why it's there. Just landing on the glass, distorting the world behind it, then sliding down and gone.

We talk so much about meaning, about the weight of words, about the responsibility to the reader. But I think I miss the point. A sentence isn't a contract. It's more like a small animal that wandered into your yard. You didn't call it. You don't fully understand why it's there. It sits in the grass, looks at you with its quick dark eyes, and then it runs.

That's all any of this is. A brief, strange visitation. I write because the silence between thoughts is too wide, and I don't know what else to do with my hands. The words come like that rain—uninvited, indifferent, gone before I can ask. And the window is just a window again. And I am just a person, sitting, listening to the drip.
